extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset for evaluating computational models' text understanding via a word prediction task using narrative passages where the last word is guessable by humans only when given the broader discourse context.
extraction.creator: Denis Papemo, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bemardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA was built by selecting narrative passages from a corpus of test novels, with passages filtered so that humans could guess the last word when given the full passage but not when given only the final sentence. A control set was also created by randomly sampling 5K similar passages from the same novels without filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Narrative passages from novels/test novels, with target final words in context; additionally, similar-shaped passages were extracted from training novels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotation was conducted via a three-step crowdsourcing protocol to filter passages: one subject guessed the target word from the full passage; if correct, a second subject also guessed from the full passage; if also correct, additional subjects guessed from the target sentence alone until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. Items were included only if two full-passage annotators exactly matched the word and no sentence-only annotator could guess it; sentence-only annotators were allowed 3 guesses, and the same subject could not judge the same item in both conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports filtering outcomes and strict validation criteria rather than inter-annotator agreement metrics: 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, 6–7% at step 2, and 3–5% at step 3; only about 1 in 25 examples passed all steps. A pilot study informed the addition of step 2 to ensure items were easy with discourse context but not local context.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 full-passage annotations per retained item, plus up to 10 sentence-only annotations; sentence-only annotators could make 3 guesses each.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A combination of four language models was used to pre-filter passages before human annotation: a pre-trained RNN, a 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is biased toward passages where the target word is strongly cued by broader discourse, often appearing in the context, and it over-represents proper nouns while under-representing other parts of speech.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset mainly captures cases where broad context strongly cues the answer, with many targets recoverable through co-reference and noun-focused phenomena; verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are rare because many such items can be guessed from local sentence context alone.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The passages are drawn from novels and may include personal or sensitive human attributes in text, such as references to health or reproductive topics.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark to evaluate computational models and language modeling architectures on text understanding and the ability to use broad discourse context for word prediction. It includes training data from disjoint novels and separate development and test passages.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus are available for download, while the test set is planned for release at the time of a public competition.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce the LAMBADA dataset ( LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects).

description.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
